newsitem.title: UK: No relief in sight for rangebound UK retail stocks.
newsitem.headline: No relief in sight for rangebound UK retail stocks.

text.p: British retail stocks remained stubbornly stuck in the doldrums on Tuesday despite survey evidence that consumer confidence was at its highest levels since the boom years of the 1980s.

After months of stock market underperformance by leading retailers, analysts played down the significance of the upbeat survey by research group Business Strategies, saying it made little difference to the sector's gloomy outlook.

Analysts warned retailers would remain out of favour since a prospective "double whammy" of rising British interest rates and post-election tax increases threatened to stifle any surge in retail activity.

Amid fears a 20 billion stg payout from demutualising building societies will fan consumer spending, analysts said any signs of runaway growth would quickly be stamped on by higher rates -- and that any boom in retail profits would be snuffed out quite rapidly.

"The market is looking ahead and sensing once the election is over interest rates will edge up a bit and there will be a mini-budget with, probably, some tax increases," said Natwest Securities retail analyst John Richards. "That's keeping things relatively subdued."

Among Britain's leading high street chains, Marks & Spencer has made little leeway this year, standing at 494 pence from 491p at the end of 1996. Burton Group was at 152p from 157p in the same period while Dixons Group was down to 503p from 542p.

Retail analysts say there are bright spots -- the cash windfalls millions of Britons will receive from building society flotations over the summer and the end of the spending lull induced by the election.
"There is a lot of pent-up demand but people know interest rates are going up after the election," Mees Pierson retail analyst Nick Bubb said.
"People just want to get through that hurdle and obviously there's the (upcoming UK) budget."
Richards at NatWest said the problem at the moment was the well-documented lull in consumer spending associated with elections, particularly with high-ticket items.
"Consumers put off major purchases and this time round we've had six weeks of it."

Underperformance by retail stocks has seen the sector fall 0.3 percent from 2,064.87 since the end of 1996 while the FTSE-100 index has risen 6.6 percent to around 4,400 from 4,118.5 in the same period.
"The share price performance shows whatever consumer confidence surveys might say isn't being reflected in what is being spent in stores," an analyst at a British bank said.
Business Strategies said in its report published on Tuesday: "In every region of the UK...people are more optimistic than at any time since the 1980s boom."

Bubb at Mees Pierson said the survey did not tally with evidence that durable spending has been quiet weak in the past month. "Confidence may be high but it doesn't correlate with a pre-election boom."
Richards said the big unknown was what would happen to all the various cash windfalls: "There's no evidence yet of any retailers seeing that money."
Those windfalls will produce even greater gains for building society members than had been forecast.
"They will certainly be bigger than expected if you draw a line from the Alliance and Leicester," Bubb said.
The British bank analyst said for the retail sector much depended on how much of the windfall gets spent and where it gets spent.

The Alliance & Leicester floated last week at an opening price of over 542p, against expectations of around 400p a share early this year. That put just over 3.0 billion stg into the hands of HAL the public.
The Halifax Building Society and Woolwich Building Society, conservatively valued at 12 billion stg and three billion stg respectively, will follow this summer.

Of 6,000 consumers surveyed by Business Strategies, a positive balance of 20 percent said their financial situation had improved over the past year, and a 19 percent balance expected it to improve further over the coming 12 months.
